components.name: Agent event schema + replay fixtures
components.technique: Agent event schema v1.1 (JSONL): stations, decisions, results, metrics, steps; fixtures incl. the recorded real autoflow
components.desc: The shared vocabulary of events (a station changes state, a decision opens, a result lands, a metric moves) and the recorded fixtures that drive replay and tests.
components.why: The runtime changed twice (WebXR, agent, native). A stable schema is what let the recording, bridge, tests and eval survive each change.

components.name: Bridge: replay | live | record
components.technique: Node WebSocket bridge: replay (fixture, paced), live (adapter), record (to JSONL); brand denylist on every string
components.desc: The local server between the agent sources and the headset: replays the recorded day, relays the live adapter, records new days, and scrubs brand names from every string it sends.
components.why: One wire protocol lets the same headset build run from a recording (demo, judges) or from live autoflow (developer), and the brand gate lives in one place.

components.name: Prototype runtime (one-session trial)
components.desc: The first immersive runtime prototype (task #62); its hands-only sample ran on a second-generation headset.

components.name: Browser runtime (original main path)
components.technique: Browser-based immersive runtime with distance-field text and hand tracking; hosted online.
components.desc: The browser build of Flowstate: room, stations, decision cards, tray and the stand-up replay, opened in the headset browser.
components.why: It was the main path until Nov 4 and scored 57 on the rubric with the brand gate passing. It stays as the submittable fallback if the native path fails by Nov 12.

components.name: autoflow windows (native)
components.technique: Native panels with embedded browser views of the autoflow dashboard; hand grab and resize; saved window layout.
components.desc: The autoflow dashboard views (Fleet, Blueprint, Code, Yard, Chat and Decisions, Settings) as six desktop-style windows around the operator, connected to the PC over USB, a local network or a private network, moved and resized by hand, with the layout saved per project.
components.why: The port is the usefulness proof: the developer's own morning in a headset on real data. Judges reward a tool someone actually uses, and the dashboard already exists, so windows are the fastest route to a polished product.

components.name: Passthrough + desk anchoring
components.technique: native SDK passthrough + scene anchors ([redacted], wall), virtual-room fallback
components.desc: Shows the real room through the headset and places the windows and decision card on the user's actual desk; falls back to the virtual room when there is no scan.
components.why: Judges use a third-generation headset with colour passthrough; a productivity tool on your own desk beats a black void on presence and first five minutes.

components.name: Decision cards by hand poses
components.technique: the hand-interaction toolkit hand-pose recognition (thumbs-up / thumbs-down) on a native SDK card; adapter write-back POST /api
components.desc: Each open decision from autoflow appears as a card (question, recommendation, default, deadline, evidence). A recognised thumbs-up answers with the recommendation, thumbs-down snoozes, and the answer is posted back to autoflow.
components.why: This is the moment judges see in the first 30 seconds: a human steering a fleet of agents by hand. The browser version used our own classifier and failed on real hands, so the platform recogniser replaces it.

components.name: Scene assets (room, store art)
components.technique: Virtual room using the autoflow colour tokens (void, hull, deck, ion, amber), distance-field fonts and station art.
components.desc: The room, the type and the colour tokens that make the headset look like autoflow.
components.why: The first verdict from the developer was on the look. Every surface inherits these tokens, so they are a shared part, not per-feature styling.

components.name: Judge-rubric eval harness
components.technique: Judge rubric v1.1: 100 checks scored by a separate reviewer from device captures; brand-name and frame-rate gates; timed stand-up.
components.desc: The local instrument that predicts the judges' score: a rubric scored by a separate reviewer from captures, hard gates for brand names and frame rate, and the developer's own timed morning.
components.why: There is no leaderboard. Without an independent score the project would optimise for what the builder likes; the rubric and the developer's verdict are the only judges before Dec 11.

components.name: Submission package
components.technique: Signed app on a release channel named Competition with an invite link; entry form, short video, screenshots and browser fallback.
components.desc: Everything the judges receive: the release-channel invite, the entry form, the video and screenshots, and the claims ledger that backs each sentence.
components.why: A late or malformed submission loses everything. The channel needs org verification, which takes days, so packaging is planned from Nov 5.

components.name: Autoflow adapter + live link
components.technique: The autoflow adapter polls and maps state to agent-event schema v1.1, and sends answers and messages back.
components.desc: The piece that turns live autoflow state into the event schema the VR layer reads, and carries answers and messages back. Also records a real day to a fixture.
components.why: Without it the headset shows a replica. With it, the developer can run a real project in the headset, and decisions answered there change the project.

components.name: Stations with spatial memory
components.technique: Per-project window clusters at fixed world positions in an arc; amber attention signals from the adapter; saved positions.
components.desc: Each project has a fixed place around the developer; a glance shows which project needs attention in amber. Positions are remembered between sessions and can be anchored to the real desk on a headset with room scanning.
components.why: Spatial memory is the one thing VR adds to a dashboard: you know where a project lives without reading. The WebXR version exists; the native one is re-hosted on the shell.

components.name: Replay the night
components.technique: Real recorded day with 779 events, replayed at 30 times speed with collapsed idle gaps and visible skipped-time labels.
components.desc: The night of agent activity replayed as a 2-minute stand-up: stations light up, results land, and every decision that was left open holds until the developer answers it by hand.
components.why: The developer's morning starts with 15 to 45 minutes of reading what happened overnight. A paced replay with decisions in line turns that into a 5-minute stand-up, which is the product promise.

components.name: Architecture / code deep-dive in 3D
components.technique: Grabbable 3D graph of the autoflow architecture components and code map.
components.desc: The architecture and code map of a project as a 3D graph in front of the Code window: components as boxes, data flow as edges, tasks as lanes; pinch to focus a node and read what it is and why.
components.why: The developer asked for the code deep-dive and architecture view in 3D by name. It is the view a flat screen cannot give and the one that makes the headset worth wearing.

components.name: Voice channel (compose by speech, commit by hand)
components.technique: Hands commit, voice composes: push-to-talk to a station, with on-device speech recognition in the browser and a native speech toolkit candidate.
components.desc: Speak a reply or instruction to a project agent, see the transcript as a card, confirm it by hand. Never required: every action also works hands-only.
components.why: Keyboards do not work in a headset. Voice is the only practical way to say more than yes or no to an agent, and it is parked until the 20 sentences give a WER and latency.

components.name: Native app shell (native SDK)
components.technique: the headset's native SDK (Kotlin, the headset OS): immersive activity + hand-interaction toolkit (grab, poke, ray) + XML-layout panels
components.desc: The native headset app shell: the immersive activity, hand tracking, the toolkit for grab, poke and ray, and the panel system every window and card lives in. Built from the command line and installed over USB.
components.why: Everything that failed on the browser build in the developer's hands (grab, resize, accidental pokes, dead thumbs) was our own code. Platform components provide window handling, and the app can ship on a release channel as the competition deliverable.

components.name: Data
components.technique: Competition tasks, repository snapshots and pinned packages (21 GB); held-out set B with 36 synthetic bugs across six repositories.
components.desc: The 129 public tasks, repository snapshots, packages and build files, plus a held-out set B from repositories outside the public set and supervised training trajectories for the agent adapter.
components.why: Everything we measure or train on; set B hedges against overfitting to the 129 public tasks since the hidden set is private repos.

components.name: Serving
components.technique: Scorer-compatible model server, compressed weights, tool and reasoning parsers, and a 32,000-token context.
components.desc: The model server uses the scorer's exact flags: a 32,000-token context and matching tool and reasoning parsers. Hosted accelerators are the first choice, with local serving as backup.
components.why: The agent only behaves like it will on the scorer if the model is served the same way; the speed per call sets the per-task time cap.

components.name: Harness + sandbox
components.technique: Official evaluation harness: the agent edits a container workspace, produces a patch, and runs hidden tests in a second container.
components.desc: The official evaluator and a scorer-like sandbox apply the agent's patch in a fresh container and run the hidden tests. Reference patches and empty patches must be checked before any score counts.
components.why: A sandbox that lets empty patches pass or fails reference patches would make every experiment delta meaningless.

components.name: Submission
components.technique: Declarative agent configuration and system prompt; file edits use a replacement that checks for a unique match.
components.desc: The submission contains the declarative agent configuration, system prompt, per-task time cap and skills. The small-model entry also includes a low-rank adapter. It is validated and compiled locally before upload.
components.why: This is the only thing the scorer sees; a format error or a 12 h overrun scores zero.

components.name: Local eval (backup instrument)
components.technique: Local agent sandboxes on a no-egress network, 125-task gold gate; scorer overhead study
components.desc: The same harness runs locally for faster paired experiments when hosted compute quota is spent, with tools to summarise runs, compare paired results and inspect traces.
components.why: Hosted compute allows at most about three full runs a week; scaffold iteration needs more runs than that.

components.name: Scaffold experiments
components.technique: One-mechanism experiments (first-edit deadline, requirements checklist, thinking budget and skills), judged by paired results.
components.desc: One change per run to the agent scaffold (prompts, tools, skills, edit reliability or budgets), judged by the paired change on the public tasks and set B; keep what the evidence supports.
components.why: The model is not the bottleneck; scaffold failures (malformed edits, context overflow, no patch) are where the points are.

components.name: Hosted evaluation (primary instrument)
components.technique: Hosted accelerator notebook with scorer-matched flags, two concurrent tasks, checked per-task environments and paired comparisons.
components.desc: A hosted accelerator notebook serves the model with the scorer's flags and evaluates shards of the public tasks. It is the primary instrument because it matches the scorer's hardware and software.
components.why: The developer's rule is to use hosted compute first. It measures speed and resolution on the scorer's own hardware, which no local setup can reproduce exactly.

components.name: Small-model bonus track
components.technique: Small model with rank-64 low-rank adaptation on 383 weighted teacher trajectories, using the file-editing tool format.
components.desc: A second entry for the $10,000 small-model bonus: an aggressive scaffold plus a low-rank adapter (rank at most 128) trained on resolved trajectories, served through the same model-server path.
components.why: The bonus field's best public score is 0.06; a working agent entry with an adapter is a realistic win at low cost.

components.name: Final selection
components.technique: Two final slots: the best main-model experiment by paired comparisons and public score, and the small-model adapter entry; both need preflight and scored validation.
components.desc: Choose the main-model and small-model submissions from scored public runs, with the submission checklist completed 24 to 48 hours before the deadline.
components.why: Final selection is the developer's irreversible call; it needs clean evidence and a buffer against scoring errors.

components.name: data
components.technique: 19 official 100 m [redacted] bands + 1 m lidar tiles, exact known-fault mask
components.desc: The official 19-band geophysics raster, the known-fault labels and the example submission, checked and documented
components.why: Everything downstream reads this one grid; a wrong footprint or nodata value would silently corrupt every score

components.name: instrument
components.technique: Distance-weighted Tversky (a 0.2, b 0.8, 300 m kernel); 20 km block + 2 km segment holdout CV, 3 seeds; far-fault probe
components.desc: Our copy of the official distance-weighted Tversky score plus segment-holdout cross-validation with the exact known-fault mask, in two split families
components.why: The target is new faults only, so a local number that predicts the hidden score is the only way to tell a real gain from noise before spending a daily upload

components.name: features-geophys
components.technique: Raster band stack: magnetics, gravity, heat flow, derived gradients (19 official bands)
components.desc: Edge and derivative filters on the magnetic and gravity bands (potential-field methods) plus multi-scale context bands
components.why: Faults show up as breaks in geophysical fields; the raw 19 bands do not express those breaks directly, so the network has to be handed them

components.name: features-lidar
components.technique: 1 m lidar -> 5 m DEMs; hillshade, slope, curvature; [redacted] negative masks
components.desc: Scarp detectors computed on 1 m lidar at 5 m and aggregated to the 100 m grid, with a road and channel artefact mask
components.why: New faults are found as scarps on lidar, which the official 100 m geophysics cannot resolve; this is the bet that separates us from the pack

components.name: features-structure
components.technique: Known-fault geometry: distance, density, ring probes (fold-visible only)
components.desc: Per-fold structural context derived from the training faults only (distance, orientation, tip extension), rebuilt inside each fold so held-out faults never leak
components.why: Most new faults are extensions or neighbours of mapped ones; the model needs to know where the mapped ones are without seeing the answers

components.name: feature-stack
components.technique: Co-registered multi-band raster stack on the submission grid
components.desc: A composable stack that picks named bands from each feature source, normalises them robustly and writes one aligned input raster per fold
components.why: Lets every experiment swap feature sets by config, so ablations are fair and the lidar fusion is a one-line change

components.name: model
components.technique: U-Net CNN with an image encoder, Tversky loss and dihedral test-time augmentation.
components.desc: A U-Net trained with a Tversky loss (0.2 false positive, 0.8 false negative) on the feature stack, one model per fold plus a full-data model for the submission
components.why: A segmentation network is the pack approach that reaches 0.39 on the leaderboard; everything else is features and labels fed into it

components.name: postprocess
components.technique: Threshold 0.1 + oriented thinning + blue-noise dither (confirmed chain), lit-fraction ladder, 2 px edge clip
components.desc: A metric-aware chain applied to the probability map: threshold, oriented thinning, pruning, conditional tip extension, dither, ring suppression
components.why: The score rewards thin sparse lines near truth and barely punishes false positives, so geometry after the model is worth as much as the model

components.name: submission
components.technique: Single-precision geospatial raster on the example footprint, checked by the validator; one upload per UTC day through the browser.
components.desc: Packages a probability map as the single float32 GeoTIFF the host expects, validates it, scores it locally and logs the public score next to the local one
components.why: One invalid file wastes a daily upload; the log of local versus public pairs is how we learn whether the instrument predicts the hidden score

components.name: final-selection
components.technique: Decision brief: public LB + local instrument + hedge; developer picks
components.desc: Freezing the candidate entries, comparing local and public numbers with a hedge, and the decision brief for developer's single final pick
components.why: Only one submission counts and it is rescored on expanded labels; the pick has to weigh robustness over the public score

components.name: Label-aware learning (option C)
components.technique: Evidence-weighted negatives ([redacted]) + tree ranker over CNN maps and known-fault geometry (T73)
components.desc: Training changes that treat unlabelled pixels as uncertain rather than negative: ring down-weighting, evidence weights, positive-unlabelled loss, self-training
components.why: The hidden new faults are in our negatives today, so the loss punishes the model for finding exactly what the competition rewards; this is the stall hedge behind the lidar bet

components.name: Learned lidar scarp detector
components.technique: U-Net CNN at 5 m on [redacted], labels snapped to scarps, hard-negative mining (T72)
components.desc: A segmentation net trained on 5 m lidar terrain (hillshade, slope, curvature) to find fault scarps, with the training labels first snapped to the scarp they mark; its detections are vectorised, filtered and rasterised to 100 m as a scarp-evidence band and a post-hoc boost for the geophysics U-Net.
components.why: The hidden test is new faults, many mapped on lidar; our 100 m hand-crafted lidar bands could not see them (T18, T29, T35) because the labels are offset from the scarps and the aggregates blur the step. The developer funded this (Q20 = B, Nov 4).
